learn.title: Start from the question
learn.body: There is no best data structure, only a good fit for what the program does most. Ask what you do often: read by position, add and remove, look up by key, keep sorted, or match word prefixes.

learn.title: What each is good at
learn.body: Array: fast access by index, costly to insert in the middle. Linked list: cheap insert and remove at a known place, slow to search. Hash table: fast lookup by key on average, no order. BST: lookup and sorted order, if it stays bushy. Trie: lookups and prefixes by letters.

learn.title: Three small decisions
learn.body: Decide which structure fits each need.
steps: A to-do pile where you only add and remove the newest: a stack
Word counts by name with quick lookup: a hash table
A word list that must suggest completions for typed letters: a trie
Names kept in sorted order, with fast search: a BST

learn.body: Start with the simplest structure that works. Switch only when measuring shows a real problem.

questions.prompt: Match each need to the best fit.
pairs: Look up a value by key quickly
questions.explanation: Each structure is strongest at one kind of job.

questions.prompt: Which structure keeps its items in sorted order as you insert?
questions.explanation: An in-order walk of a BST gives sorted values.

questions.prompt: A hash table is bad at...
questions.explanation: The hash scatters keys, so order is lost.

questions.prompt: You must undo actions in reverse order of doing them. Which fits?
questions.explanation: Undo takes the newest action first, which is last in, first out.

questions.prompt: Jobs should run in the order they arrive, so use a \_\_.
questions.explanation: A queue serves the oldest item first.

questions.prompt: A BST fed sorted data behaves like...
questions.explanation: Every insert goes the same way, giving a chain.

questions.prompt: What is the first thing to do when choosing?
choices: Think about which operations happen most
questions.explanation: The most frequent operation should be the cheap one.
